# Dimension-free capped exponentials: an exact escape reduction

All exponential variables below are independent and have mean one. For k>=1 and 0<=p<=1 define

    G_(k,p)=Pr(Gamma(k)+p Exp(1)>=Exp(1)+k+p-1).       (1)

Fix a real c<1/2. Suppose that

    G_(k,p)>=c for every integer k>=1 and p in[0,1]. (2)

Then for every finite family of coefficients

    a_0=-1,   -1<=a_i<=1,   sum_i a_i=0,

one has

    Pr(sum_i a_i E_i>=0)>=c.                         (3)

This is a complete implication with the explicit scalar hypothesis (2). It does not assert that (2), the stronger dimension-dependent angular target, or OC has been proved. Its purpose is to reduce a dimension-free coefficient bound to the deterministic-negative family (1).

The inputs already proved in separate sources are:

* `candidate 9dace055ddbb6578`: compactness, continuity, and the classification of coefficient minimizers. A minimizer is either in the all-unit-negative stratum, has all positive coefficients equal to one, or has the pattern (1^k,p) against (1,b^m), with 0<p,b<1, b=(k+p-1)/m. In the latter case it has no zero coefficient, so its total number of coordinates is k+m+2.
* `candidate a6e6fd61fe60c16a`: the all-unit-negative stratum has probability at least 1/2, and a pattern with k positive units has probability at least G_(k,0).

The first source uses the second in treating its all-unit-negative boundary. Every coefficient transformation in these inputs keeps the fixed negative unit coefficient.

## 1. Uniform normal limit when the number of positive units diverges

Consider the fractional family

    V=Gamma(k)+p E_+-E_--b Gamma(m),
    b=(k+p-1)/m,   0<=p<=1, 0<=b<=1.

It is centered. Let sigma^2=Var(V)=k+p^2+1+mb^2. Then

    k+1<=sigma^2<=2(k+1).                             (4)

The upper bound follows because every coefficient has magnitude at most one, and the sums of the positive and negative coefficients both equal k+p.

As k tends to infinity, uniformly in all admissible m,p,b,

    Pr(V>=0) -> 1/2.                                 (5)

Here is an elementary characteristic-function proof, including the passage from characteristic functions to the sign probability. Write V as a sum of a_i(E_i-1), and put Z=V/sigma. A centered unit exponential has characteristic function exp(-iu)/(1-iu). For |u|<=1/2, its logarithm satisfies

    log[exp(-iu)/(1-iu)]=-u^2/2+R(u),
    |R(u)|<=2|u|^3/3.

This follows directly by summing the power series of -log(1-iu); the linear terms cancel. For each fixed real t, (4) gives

    log phi_Z(t)=-t^2/2+O(|t|^3/sigma),

uniformly in the remaining parameters, since

    sum_i |a_i|^3 <= sum_i a_i^2=sigma^2.

Thus phi_Z(t)->exp(-t^2/2) pointwise.

We can pass directly to the sign probability without invoking an unproved limit interchange. The k positive unit phases give

    |phi_Z(t)|<=(1+t^2/sigma^2)^(-k/2).

For 0<=t<=sigma, log(1+t^2/sigma^2)>=t^2/(2sigma^2), hence by (4)

    |phi_Z(t)|<=exp(-t^2/16).

For t>=sigma, substituting u=t/sigma and using 1+u^2>=2u gives

    integral_sigma^infinity |phi_Z(t)|/t dt
       <= integral_1^infinity (1+u^2)^(-k/2)/u du
       <= (2/k) 2^(-k/2).                            (6)

Near zero, |Im phi_Z(t)|/t<=E|Z|<=1. On 1<=t<=sigma the integrand is bounded by exp(-t^2/16)/t, which is integrable independently of k. Since the limiting characteristic function is real, dominated convergence on this range, followed by (6), proves

    integral_0^infinity Im phi_Z(t)/t dt ->0.          (7)

For completeness, the sign inversion identity used here is

    Pr(Z>=0)=1/2+(1/pi) integral_0^infinity
                                      Im phi_Z(t)/t dt.       (8)

There is no atom at zero because V includes the independent continuous term -E_-. To derive (8), first insert exp(-epsilon t) in the integral. Fubini is justified near zero by E|Z|<infinity and at infinity by the exponential damping. The inner sine integral is arctan(Z/epsilon), as follows by differentiation with respect to Z and integration of epsilon/(epsilon^2+Z^2), with value zero at Z=0. Bounded convergence then takes its expectation to (pi/2)E sign(Z). The undamped integral exists absolutely by the estimates above and can be recovered by dominated convergence as epsilon decreases to zero. This proves (8), and (7) proves (5).

## 2. Escape in the number of negative phases with k fixed

Let k be fixed, m_j->infinity, p_j->p in[0,1], and b_j=(k+p_j-1)/m_j. Then

    Pr(Gamma(k)+p_j E_+>=E_-+b_j Gamma(m_j))
          ->G_(k,p).                                 (9)

Indeed the negative gamma term has mean k+p_j-1 and variance
(k+p_j-1)^2/m_j, so it converges in probability to k+p-1. Couple the fixed gamma and exponential variables and use the same E_+ for every p_j; the positive term then converges almost surely. The limiting difference includes -E_- independently and therefore has no atom at zero.

One can justify the probability limit without any continuity shorthand: for every delta>0, outside an event with probability tending to zero the two differences differ by at most delta. The probability difference is therefore bounded in the limit by the probability that the limiting difference lies in[-delta,delta]. This decreases to zero with delta because of the absence of an atom at zero. Thus (9) holds, including p=0 and p=1.

## 3. Compact minimizers and the dimension-free implication

For d>=1, let A_d be the compact coefficient set with d+1 coordinates, a_0=-1, all coefficients in[-1,1], and total sum zero. Put

    c_d=min_(a in A_d) Pr(sum_i a_i E_i>=0).

Continuity and existence of this minimum are proved in the boundary-stratum source, or follow directly by coupling and the continuous independent term -E_0. Padding a coefficient vector with a zero embeds A_d into A_(d+1), leaving its probability unchanged. Thus c_d is nonincreasing and has a limit alpha>=0.

Suppose (3) is false. Then alpha<c; choose d_0 with c_(d_0)<c. For every d>=d_0 choose a minimizer. The all-unit-negative stratum is excluded by its lower bound 1/2>c. The all-unit-positive stratum is excluded by its lower bound G_(k,0)>=c, which follows from (2). Therefore every such minimizer has the fractional pattern

    positive (1^k_d,p_d), negative (1,b_d^m_d),
    0<p_d,b_d<1,
    b_d=(k_d+p_d-1)/m_d,
    k_d+m_d+2=d+1.                                   (10)

The last equality is crucial: there are no zero coordinates at a fractional minimizer. It is a proved consequence of the strict multiplier inequality q<1, not a dimension-count assumption.

The sequence k_d is bounded. Otherwise some subsequence has k_d->infinity, and Section 1 forces its probabilities c_d to tend to 1/2. This contradicts c_d<=c_(d_0)<c<1/2.

Pass to a subsequence on which k_d is a fixed integer k, and then to a further subsequence on which p_d converges to p in[0,1]. Equation (10) forces m_d->infinity. Section 2 gives

    alpha=lim c_d=G_(k,p)>=c,

contradicting alpha<c. This proves (3).

No infimum over dimensions was assumed to be attained. The two possible escapes are explicitly handled: k diverging gives a uniform normal limit, while m diverging with k fixed gives the stated deterministic-negative law. All finite-dimensional minima, all boundary probabilities, and every limiting sign comparison have been justified.
